title: Rate limiting, overload and resilience patterns
summary: Every service has a finite capacity and demand will sometimes exceed it. This lesson measures overload as lost goodput, limits each caller with token buckets, sliding windows and concurrency limits, places the limits locally, globally and per tenant, answers with 429, Retry-After and the RateLimit fields, sheds load by criticality on a utilisation signal, sizes queues and adapts concurrency limits, throttles in the client, isolates dependencies with bulkheads and proxy circuit breakers, and removes modes with static stability and constant work, ending with a decision table and a degradation ladder for one service's overload plan.

blocks.text: Stripe runs four limiters in production: a per-user request rate limiter on token buckets in Redis that rejects millions of requests a month, mostly runaway test-mode scripts; a concurrent requests limiter that fixed contention on its most expensive endpoints; a fleet usage shedder that reserves a fraction of the fleet for critical methods and rejects non-critical requests beyond their share with a 503; and a worker utilisation shedder that drops test-mode traffic, then GETs, then other POSTs, slowly enough not to flap. Every limiter fails open and was dark-launched before it was enforced.

Cloudflare enforces per-domain rate limits inside each point of presence rather than globally, relying on anycast to bring a client to the same location, and approximates a sliding window from two fixed-window counters in a consistent-hashed memcached cluster; across 400 million requests the approximation misjudged 0.003 percent of them.

Google's RPC system carries a four-level criticality on every request, propagates it by default to the calls a request makes, sheds from the lowest level when a task's executor load average passes its processors, enforces per-customer quotas in CPU rather than queries, and throttles in the client once attempted requests exceed twice the accepted ones over a two-minute window.

Amazon's services measure goodput rather than throughput, keep prioritisation heuristics consistent across the services that cooperate on one request and shift crawler traffic off peak, give in-quota requests priority over another client's burst, skip the remaining work when the client has already timed out, keep enough spare capacity to lose an Availability Zone without scaling, and load-test far beyond the breaking point so that goodput is seen to plateau rather than collapse.

Netflix's services set their concurrency limits adaptively with the concurrency-limits library, treating the limit as a TCP congestion window: a delay-based Vegas or Gradient2 limiter on the server and a loss-based AIMD limiter in the client, so that a retry storm or a slow dependency lowers the admitted concurrency instead of filling the queues.

subtopics.title: Overload, goodput and why queries per second mislead

blocks.text: Every service has a finite capacity and demand will sometimes exceed it: a traffic spike, one misbehaving client, a dependency that slows down, or capacity lost to a failure. The Builders' Library describes what overload looks like from the inside. Latency at high utilisation is higher than at low utilisation because thread contention, context switching, garbage collection and I/O contention grow with load, until the server reaches an inflection point past which it degrades faster than the load grows. The useful measure is goodput: the subset of the throughput that is handled without errors and fast enough for the client to use the response. Past the inflection point throughput keeps rising and goodput falls.

The reason it falls to zero rather than to a plateau is a feedback loop. When a client times out, the server has usually still done the work, so the capacity was spent for nothing; the client retries, which adds load; and the service becomes modal, behaving one way under normal load and another, worse way under stress. The whole toolkit in this lesson exists to break that loop: reject early and cheaply, reject the least important work first, and stop the demand at its source before it reaches the network.

The SRE book adds a warning about the unit of capacity. Queries per second is a poor measure because queries differ wildly in cost, and the mix changes over time; Google learned to model capacity in resources, usually CPU, and to measure each request's cost as the CPU time it consumed. A limit expressed in requests per second is therefore a proxy, good for a single endpoint with uniform requests and misleading for a service whose expensive calls are a small fraction of its traffic.

blocks.text: Measure goodput, not throughput, and load-test past the point where the service breaks. The Builders' Library's rule is that a service that has not been tested far beyond its breaking point will fail in the least desirable way.

subtopics.title: Rate limiting algorithms: buckets and windows

blocks.text: The token bucket is the workhorse. Stripe describes it as a bucket per user into which tokens drip at a fixed rate; each request takes a token and is rejected when the bucket is empty. The drip rate is the sustained limit and the capacity is the burst a caller may spend at once, so one mechanism expresses both. A fixed window counts requests per calendar interval and resets, which is cheap but lets a caller spend two windows' worth across a boundary. A leaky bucket drains a counter at the allowed rate and caps it at the burst; Cloudflare notes it is what the stock NGINX module uses and that it needs operations that are hard to make atomic in a shared store.

Cloudflare's limiter runs at every edge location against a shared memcached store whose only operations are get, set and atomic increment, so it needed an algorithm built from counters: a sliding window approximated from two fixed windows, the current window's count plus the previous window's count weighted by how much of it still falls inside the sliding interval. Against 400 million requests from 270,000 sources the approximation wrongly allowed or limited 0.003 percent of requests, with an average difference of 6 percent between the real and the approximated rate.

blocks.title: Cloudflare's sliding window approximation, with the post's numbers.
items: The limit on the endpoint is 50 requests per minute.
The current minute started 15 seconds ago and has seen 18 requests.
The previous minute still covers 45 of the sliding 60 seconds, so its weight is 45 / 60 = 0.75.
The approximate rate is 42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 requests, so the next request is the one that trips the limit.

blocks.caption: The algorithms compared.
rows: the capacity, then the drip rate
per-caller limits with a burst allowance
up to twice the limit at a boundary
a level and a drain time

blocks.text: Stripe's second limiter shows why a rate is not always the right quantity. Instead of a thousand requests per second it says a caller may have 20 requests in progress at once. That contains callers who send few but heavy requests and those who retry on timeout and stack up work, and it solved the contention on Stripe's most expensive endpoints; the cost is a worker-pool programming model for callers instead of send and back off.

subtopics.title: Where the limits live: local, global and per tenant

blocks.text: A limit enforced inside each instance from an in-memory bucket is fast, has no dependency and keeps working through a partition, but it is a limit per instance, so the effective fleet-wide limit grows with the instance count and a caller whose traffic is balanced across the fleet is bounded only loosely. A global limit keeps the counters in a shared store and answers allow or deny per request or per connection for a set of descriptors such as the caller, the route or a header value; it is precise and it puts a round trip to a store on the request path.

blocks.legend: The layered defence: a global per-tenant limit at the gateway backed by a shared counter store, a local token bucket and per-upstream circuit-breaker limits in the proxy, and utilisation-based shedding by criticality inside the service. The pieces follow Stripe's limiters, Envoy's circuit breaking and the SRE book's shedding (s1, s12, s6).

blocks.text: Both Stripe and Cloudflare put the shared counters close to the request. Stripe runs its buckets in Redis behind the API and hooks the limiters into the middleware so that an exception in the limiting code or a Redis outage fails open and the API keeps serving. Cloudflare could not centralise counters across its anycast network, so it counts inside each point of presence: anycast delivers a given client address to the same location under normal conditions, and a consistent-hashed memcached cluster inside that location shares the counters among its servers. The limit is therefore enforced per location, which is precise enough because the client's traffic lands there.

blocks.caption: Google's per-customer limits as the SRE book illustrates them: a backend with 10,000 CPUs worldwide hands out quotas by customer, and the quotas add up to more than the capacity because customers do not peak together.

blocks.text: Per-tenant limits are the edge's main job in a shared service. The SRE book's version provisions the backend from negotiated usage, defines a quota per customer in CPU rather than requests, aggregates global usage from every task in real time and pushes effective limits back to the tasks, so that in a global overload only the customers over their quota see errors. The common design uses both layers: a coarse local limit absorbs bursts and protects the counter store, and the global limit applies the precise per-tenant quota.

A rejected request must be cheap for the server and informative for the client. The status code is 429 Too Many Requests, which RFC 6585 defines as the user having sent too many requests in a given amount of time; the response should include details explaining the condition and may carry a Retry-After header saying how long to wait. The RFC deliberately does not say how the server identifies the user or counts the requests, so per key, per address, per resource or across a set of servers are all conformant.

What the client could not know from a bare 429 is the policy: how big the quota is, over what window, and how much is left. The IETF HTTPAPI working group's draft standardises two response fields for that. RateLimit-Policy advertises the quota policies the server applies, each with a quota, a window in seconds and optionally a partition key and a quota unit; RateLimit reports the quota currently available under a named policy. A client that reads them can pace itself before it is throttled instead of discovering the limit by hitting it.

blocks.caption: What a throttling response carries, and the source of each element.
rows: rate limited; not a server fault
seconds (or a date) before the next attempt
nothing remaining; the window resets in 12 seconds
a problem document with a documentation link
which limit was hit and what to do

blocks.text: Two operational rules come with the headers. First, fail open: Stripe catches exceptions at every level of its limiting code so that a bug or a store outage never turns the limiter into the outage, which means a limit that protects something that must not be exceeded needs an explicit fail-closed flag. Second, dark-launch every new limiter: run it in a mode that only logs what it would have rejected, inspect that traffic, tune the thresholds and talk to the callers whose patterns would break before enforcing it. Alerts and metrics on how often each limiter fires come with the launch, not after it.

A 429 without Retry-After or the RateLimit fields trains clients to retry immediately, which turns the limiter into a source of load. Say when to come back, and make the limiter's rejection far cheaper than the work it refuses.

Rate limits protect against individual callers; load shedding protects against total demand exceeding capacity when every caller is inside its limit. The SRE book makes criticality a first-class property of every request in Google's RPC system, with four values, and uses it in every control: when a customer runs out of quota a backend rejects a criticality only once it is already rejecting all lower ones, an overloaded task rejects lower criticalities sooner, and the criticality is propagated by default from a request to the calls it makes, so a deep dependency sheds consistently with the frontend's decision. The practice is to set it as close to the user as possible, typically in the HTTP frontends.

blocks.caption: Two criticality ladders in production: Google's four values and Stripe's four shedding categories, each dropped from the bottom up.
rows: CRITICAL_PLUS: serious user-visible impact if it fails
critical methods, such as creating a charge
CRITICAL: the default for production jobs; user-visible impact
SHEDDABLE_PLUS: partial unavailability expected; the default for batch jobs
SHEDDABLE: frequent partial and occasional full unavailability expected

blocks.text: The signal that triggers shedding is utilisation, and Google's most useful one is the executor load average: the number of threads running or ready to run, smoothed with exponential decay, with rejection beginning as it grows past the processors available to the task. The smoothing swallows a brief fan-out spike and reacts to sustained load. Stripe watches the number of workers with spare capacity and sheds slowly from the bottom tier up, bringing traffic back just as slowly, because shedding and restoring quickly makes the system flap between healthy and awful.

Stripe runs a second shedder ahead of utilisation: a fleet usage shedder that reserves a fraction of the fleet for critical requests, counted in Redis, so that when the reservation is 20 percent any non-critical request beyond the other 80 percent is rejected with a 503 before the workers are busy. The Builders' Library adds two rules about the decision: when many services cooperate on one request, conflicting prioritisation heuristics between them waste work and hurt availability, so the ordering is agreed once rather than invented per service; and a client that bursts above its quota is served at a lower priority than other clients' within-quota requests.

Rejection must be much cheaper than service, so shed before parsing a large body or taking a lock, and check the clock: a server that notices the client has already timed out skips the rest of the work.

subtopics.title: Queues, adaptive concurrency limits and client-side throttling

blocks.text: Most servers put a queue in front of a pool of workers, and the queue is where overload hides. The SRE book's arithmetic: if the queue holds ten times the thread count and a request takes 100 milliseconds on a thread, a request that finds the queue full takes 1.1 seconds, almost all of it queueing, and its caller has often given up. For steady traffic the advice is a queue of at most half the pool size, so the server rejects early; a last-in-first-out or controlled-delay queue sheds the requests whose callers have most likely abandoned them.

blocks.title: Sizing the queue from the SRE book's figures.
items: A server has 64 worker threads and a service time of 100 ms per request.
At the book's example ratio of a queue ten times the threads, the queue holds 640 requests and a request at the back waits 640 / 64 × 100 ms = 1 second before its 100 ms of work.
At the recommended ratio of half the pool, the queue holds 32 requests and the worst queueing delay is 32 / 64 × 100 ms = 50 ms.
Beyond that, the server returns 503 at once, which the cascading-failures chapter gives as the simplest per-task shedding rule: reject when more than a set number of requests are in flight.

blocks.text: The right in-flight limit is hard to set by hand because it depends on the hardware and moves as the fleet scales. Netflix's concurrency-limits library derives it from Little's law, limit = average rate × average latency, and estimates it the way TCP estimates a congestion window. The Vegas limit estimates the queue as L × (1 - minRTT / sampleRTT), raising the limit by one per window while the estimated queue is under a small alpha and lowering it when over a slightly larger beta; Gradient2 compares a short and a long exponential average of latency to detect a queueing trend; a loss-based AIMD limit on the client backs off on timeouts and rejections. The README recommends a delay-based limiter on the server and a loss-based or combined one on the client.

Client-side adaptive throttling closes the loop from the other end. Each Google client task keeps two counts over the last two minutes, requests attempted and requests accepted, and once requests exceed K times accepts it rejects new requests locally with a probability that grows with the gap. The usual K is 2: the backend still sees about twice what it accepts, which wastes some capacity but lets clients notice recovery quickly; a K of 1.1 wastes less and recovers more slowly. The decision uses only local information, so it adds no dependency and no latency.
Pair a small queue with a measured concurrency limit on the server and adaptive throttling in the client library. Together they mean an overloaded backend sees shrinking demand, not growing demand.

subtopics.title: Bulkheads, proxy circuit breakers, static stability and constant work

blocks.text: A bulkhead, named for the sealed compartments of a ship's hull, isolates resources so that one consumer or one dependency cannot sink the rest. The Azure pattern partitions service instances into groups by consumer load and availability requirements, and has consumers partition their own resources, such as connection pools, per dependency, so that a slow service exhausts only its own allotment.

blocks.caption: Envoy's per-upstream circuit breaking limits, which are bulkheads at the proxy: each is tracked per upstream cluster and per routing priority, and each overflow increments a counter.
rows: connections Envoy opens to all hosts of the cluster, active or draining
the connection overflow counter rises; a selected host still gets at least one connection
requests queued while waiting for a connection
the request is failed immediately rather than queued
requests outstanding to the cluster at once
fail fast; the limit that caps in-flight work
retries outstanding to the cluster at once
the retry is dropped; the documentation recommends retry budgets instead of a static count, and aggressive breaking if static

blocks.text: Because the limits are per priority, a high-priority route gets its own pool and a flood on a low-priority route cannot starve it; and because they are observable as statistics, including the resources remaining before each one opens, they are tuned from data: start from the observed peak concurrency per upstream plus headroom, watch the overflow counters and adjust. The active-retries limit, or the retry budget Envoy recommends in its place, is the mesh-layer guard against the retry storms the idempotency lesson describes.

Two Amazon patterns remove the modes rather than manage them. Static stability means the system keeps working when a dependency is impaired, because the capacity was provisioned before the failure rather than launched in reaction to it: across three Availability Zones Amazon overprovisions by 50 percent, so each zone runs at two thirds of its tested load and the loss of a whole zone requires no action beyond health checks removing its instances. Constant work means doing the same amount of work regardless of load or stress: Route 53's health-check aggregators push a fixed-size table of every check's status to the DNS servers every few seconds whether anything changed or not, so a wave of failures costs no more than a quiet day. The article's three features of such designs are that they do not scale with load, have no modes, and if anything do less work under stress.

Prefer a design whose cost does not depend on the failure. Pre-provision for the loss you expect, push fixed-size state on a fixed cadence, and give every dependency its own pool so that a bad day for one is not a bad day for all.

subtopics.title: Writing the overload plan for one service

blocks.text: An overload plan says, for one service, which limits apply to whom, in what order load is shed, what degraded modes exist, and what the client is told at each step. The decision block chooses the primary protection per situation; most services end up with several.

blocks.caption: Choosing the protection for one service.

rows.option: per-caller rate limit (token bucket) at the gateway
rows.pick_when: callers can space their requests without changing the outcome, one caller's spike must not affect the rest, and quotas are part of the product
rows.avoid_when: the caller cannot space requests (real-time events), or request costs vary so much that a count means little
rows.example: a public API with per-key quotas; the first limiter to build

rows.option: concurrency limit per caller or per server
rows.pick_when: a few expensive or slow requests dominate, callers retry on timeout and stack up work, or in-flight work is measurable where the right rate is not
rows.avoid_when: requests are uniform and short, where a rate is simpler to explain
rows.example: export endpoints; the server-side adaptive limit

rows.option: load shedding by criticality on a utilisation signal
rows.pick_when: total demand can exceed capacity with every caller in quota, and requests have a usable importance order
rows.avoid_when: every request is equally critical and the only honest answer is more capacity
rows.example: a shared backend serving interactive and batch callers

rows.option: client-side adaptive throttling in the client library
rows.pick_when: many client tasks share a backend, rejections cost nearly as much as service, and clients send steadily enough to learn
rows.avoid_when: clients call sporadically and cannot build a local view
rows.example: internal RPC clients of a storage service

rows.pick_when: the dependency is a zone, a region or a control plane, and reacting after the failure is too slow
rows.avoid_when: capacity is too expensive to hold idle and the failure is tolerable
rows.example: a data plane that must survive a zone loss without a scale-up

blocks.caption: A degradation ladder, from the SRE book's degraded responses and the shedding tiers above: each rung costs the user something and saves the service more.
rows: test, crawler and batch traffic is shed or shifted off peak
reads are served from a local, possibly stale copy instead of the canonical store
expensive features are reduced: a search runs over a fraction of the corpus, a page drops its recommendations
non-critical writes and low-tier callers get 429 or 503 with Retry-After
the affected callers, with a reason and a time
only critical-plus traffic is served; everything else is rejected cheaply
most users, briefly, instead of everyone for longer

blocks.text: The plan is tested, not assumed. Load tests run far past saturation, checking that goodput stays flat while offered throughput rises; a variant drives steady load at a shrinking fleet; and every limiter and shedder is dark-launched first and watched through its metrics. The plan also states what the client is told at each rung, because a degraded mode the client cannot tell from a failure will be retried as one.

worked_example.title: Worked example: the overload plan for a search API behind a gateway

blocks.text: A search API serves interactive users, a few partners with batch scripts and an internal crawler, from a fleet behind a gateway. The example sets the per-tenant limits, the concurrency and queue settings, the shedding order and the provisioning, using the figures the sources give where they give them and stated assumptions elsewhere.

blocks.title: Writing the plan
items: Capacity in the SRE book's units: the fleet has 100 tasks that each handle 500 requests per second at the tested load, so the balancer admits at most 50,000 requests per second to the datacenter and the plan works in CPU seconds below that.

Per-tenant quotas at the gateway: interactive users share a pool and each partner key gets a token bucket of 200 requests per second with a burst of 400, dark-launched for a week and then enforced with a 429 that carries Retry-After and the RateLimit fields.
Concurrency for the heavy endpoint: the export endpoint allows 10 requests in progress per key, following Stripe's second limiter, because a single export holds a worker for seconds.
Queue per task: 64 workers and a 100 ms service time give a queue of 32 (half the pool), so the worst queueing delay is 50 ms and the task returns 503 beyond 96 requests in flight.

Criticality: requests are tagged at the gateway as critical (interactive search), sheddable-plus (partner batch) or sheddable (the crawler), and the tag is propagated to the index and ranking services.

Shedding: when the executor load average of a task exceeds its 8 cores, it rejects sheddable traffic first, then sheddable-plus, and critical only when both are gone; the crawler is also shifted to the off-peak window.
Client-side throttling: the internal client library tracks requests against accepts over 2 minutes and rejects locally once requests exceed 2 × accepts.
Static stability: the fleet is spread over 3 zones and overprovisioned by 50 percent, so 150 tasks are deployed and a zone loss leaves 100 tasks, the full tested capacity, with no scale-up.

Test: a load test drives offered load to 3 times the capacity and checks that goodput for critical traffic stays at the full 50,000 requests per second while the rejection counters, not the latency, absorb the excess.

blocks.code:
import time

class SlidingWindowLimiter:
    """Cloudflare's approximation: the current window's count plus the previous
    window's count weighted by how much of it is still inside the sliding interval.
    Only increments and reads are needed, so it works on a shared counter store."""

    def __init__(self, limit, window_s=60):
        self.limit, self.window = limit, window_s
        self.counts = {}            # (key, window_index) -> count

    def allow(self, key, now=None):
        now = time.time() if now is None else now
        idx = int(now // self.window)
        elapsed = now - idx * self.window
        current = self.counts.get((key, idx), 0)
        previous = self.counts.get((key, idx - 1), 0)
        weight = (self.window - elapsed) / self.window
        rate = previous * weight + current
        if rate >= self.limit:
            return False, max(0.0, self.window - elapsed)   # denied, seconds until the window turns
        self.counts[(key, idx)] = current + 1
        return True, 0.0


limiter = SlidingWindowLimiter(limit=50, window_s=60)
# the post's example: 42 in the previous minute, 18 so far, 15 s into the minute
limiter.counts[("k", 100)] = 42
limiter.counts[("k", 101)] = 18
print(limiter.allow("k", now=101 * 60 + 15))   # (True, 0.0): 42 * 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 < 50
print(limiter.allow("k", now=101 * 60 + 16))   # (False, 44.0): the 50th request is refused
blocks.caption: The sliding window approximation from the Cloudflare post as a per-key limiter; the second return value is what to send as Retry-After.

sim.heading: Simulate it
sim.caption: A token-bucket limiter admits at most its limit per second plus a burst, and turns the rest away before they reach the API. Failed in the readouts includes the requests the limiter refused.
steps: At the start 150 requests a second pass untouched and the API is about 63% busy.
Raise the offered load to 600 with the limit at 200: goodput holds at 200 requests a second, p99 stays near 81 ms and the API stays at about 83% busy, while about 67% of requests are turned away.
Raise the limit to 400, above what the API can serve, and the limiter no longer protects it: the API saturates, p99 climbs to about 288 ms and goodput falls to about 239 requests a second.
Set the offered load to 190, the limit to 200 and drop the burst to 6: even below the limit about 6% of requests are turned away, because arrivals come in clumps that a tiny bucket cannot absorb.
Raise the burst to 50 and they all pass again.
